title: Introducing Owl: a signal watcher for your pipeline
summary: Watch external changes and signals from customer conversations, then bring relevant drafts and next steps into the rep’s inbox.
body_markdown:
Most stalled deals do not come with an announcement that it is time to follow up. A company launches a product. A team starts hiring. A deadline mentioned three months ago gets closer. A buyer returns to material you sent after the last meeting.


Each change might give you a useful reason to reconnect. The hard part is noticing it across your pipeline, remembering what it means for that particular account, and turning it into something more helpful than “just checking in.”


Meet Owl, Cedar’s watcher. Owl combines external changes around your prospects with the internal signals you learn through customer conversations. It helps bring relevant changes back into your working day, along with the context and next steps to act on them.


## Start with the deals and changes you care about


In the launch demo, we ask Cedar to watch stalling deals for new launches, company news, growth in sales headcount, and new sales job postings.


That request starts with a sales question: which of these accounts might have a fresh reason to talk? It also defines what would count as relevant evidence. A company hiring salespeople may be worth revisiting if scaling its sales process was part of the earlier conversation. The same job posting might mean very little to a deal that stalled for a completely different reason.


Cedar uses the request to choose the deals, select the relevant agents, and set up watchers for the companies and people involved. You can describe the work in terms of your pipeline instead of rebuilding a separate monitoring list for every account.


The advantage is coverage with a purpose. You are asking Cedar to keep track of a particular change for a particular group of deals, so the result starts closer to a sales decision than a general news feed does.


## Turn the change into a relevant follow-up


Finding a signal is only the first step. In the demo, Cedar takes a new signal, looks at what was actually discussed with the customer, and uses that context to draft a personalized revival email.


The earlier conversation matters because it explains why the update could be useful. If a buyer described the difficulty of onboarding a growing team, a hiring push gives you something specific to revisit. If the conversation was about a capability they needed before moving ahead, a relevant launch gives you a different opening.


Those are illustrative examples of the connection: what changed, what the buyer told you, and why the two belong in the same message. A company announcement on its own does not explain that relationship.


This gives the rep a more useful starting point for a follow-up. The draft can connect to an existing problem or commitment, and the rep can decide whether that connection is strong enough to use. For a closer look at reopening an old conversation, see the[Pipeline Revival launch](https://mail.cedarcopilot.com/blog/pipeline-revival-launch) .


## Choose the external signals that matter to your sale


The launch walks through several kinds of changes Owl can watch: growth in company or department headcount, specific job postings, job changes and promotions, social posts, relevant company or industry news, and changes to a webpage such as a prospect’s changelog.


These signals answer different questions. Headcount growth can help you spot a team entering a new stage. A job posting can reveal work the company is prioritizing. A change in role can affect who is involved in a buying decision. A changelog can show how a product is evolving.


Specificity makes those signals more useful. “Watch hiring” is a broad request. Watching for growth in the sales team, or for a particular role connected to a problem discussed in discovery, gives the watcher a clearer job.


The same principle applies to news and website changes. The goal is to notice updates that have a plausible connection to the account’s situation. You can start with a narrow question, then adjust what you watch as your understanding of the deal improves.


For a rep managing an active pipeline, that helps spread attention across accounts without requiring a daily round of manual checks. The watcher keeps looking while the rep is in meetings, working a live opportunity, or preparing the next conversation.


## Remember the signals you earned in conversation


External signals are only part of the launch. Owl also brings back the information you learn by interacting with prospects.


A buyer may mention a project timeline or a competitor’s renewal date. A conversation may reveal an expansion opportunity, or a concern that could become a retention risk. Someone may return to an email or collateral sent through Cedar after a deal has gone quiet.


These signals are valuable because they come with relationship history. A renewal date means more when you know which concern prompted the buyer to consider alternatives. An upcoming project means more when you know what the team needs to accomplish and who is responsible for it.


The challenge is keeping that information useful after the meeting ends. A note can remain accurate while becoming easy to overlook. A timeline that felt distant in September can become urgent later, even if nobody sends a new email to remind you.


Owl helps those earlier details become signals for later action. The value is in bringing the relevant context back when it can affect the next step, rather than requiring the rep to remember every date and comment across every account.


An engagement event still needs interpretation. An email open or a return to a document is a reason to look at the surrounding deal context; it does not, by itself, establish that the buyer is ready to purchase. The useful question is what that activity means alongside the conversation you have already had.


## Put the next step where the rep is working


The launch ends in the rep’s inbox. Cedar brings internal signals, drafts, next steps, and tasks to the top of the working queue.


That placement matters. A signal can be correct and still have little effect if it sits in a separate dashboard that nobody checks. Bringing the change into the same place as the follow-up reduces the distance between noticing something and deciding what to do about it.


The rep should be able to understand why the account has returned to their attention: a relevant change occurred, an earlier timeline is approaching, or fresh activity deserves a closer look. The accompanying draft or task gives that attention somewhere to go.


This also connects the watcher to Cedar’s broader workspace. The account context, the conversation, and the next action can stay together as the deal develops.[Cedar Blocks](https://mail.cedarcopilot.com/blog/cedar-blocks) explains how the data, intelligence, tools, and workspace layers fit into that system.


## Give your follow-up a reason


Owl is built around a simple sales habit: reach out when you have something relevant to say. Across a full pipeline, keeping that habit takes more memory and monitoring than a rep can comfortably do alone.


By connecting external changes with the signals already present in your customer conversations, Owl helps you find a reason to revive an old deal, revisit a commitment, or prepare a useful next step.
